Did You Forget What I Asked?
Prospective Memory Failures in Large Language Models

Avni Mittal Affiliation: Microsoft Email: avnimittal@microsoft.com
Abstract

Large language models often fail to satisfy formatting instructions when they must simultaneously perform demanding tasks. We study this behavior through a prospective memory-inspired lens from cognitive psychology, using a controlled paradigm that combines verifiable formatting constraints with benchmark tasks of increasing complexity. Across three model families and over 8,000 prompts, compliance drops by 2–21% under concurrent task load. Vulnerability is highly type-dependent: terminal constraints (requiring action at the response boundary) degrade most, with drops up to 50%, while avoidance constraints remain comparatively robust. A salience-enhanced format (explicit instruction framing plus a trailing reminder) recovers much of the lost compliance, restoring performance to 90–100% in many settings. Interference is bidirectional: formatting constraints can also reduce task accuracy, with one model’s GSM8K accuracy dropping from 93% to 27%. In additional stacking experiments, joint compliance declines sharply as constraints accumulate. All results use deterministic programmatic checkers, with no LLM-as-judge component, on publicly available datasets.

1 Introduction

Large language models are increasingly used in settings where users provide behavioral or formatting constraints alongside substantive requests. A typical prompt might ask for an explanation while also requiring a specific output form (e.g., all capitals, a required ending phrase, or a fixed number of bullets). Users expect the model to preserve such constraints throughout generation. In practice, models often produce strong content while violating the requested format.

We study this pattern as a functional analog of prospective memory (PM): remembering to execute a deferred intention at the appropriate future point Einstein et al. (2005). In humans, PM failures increase under cognitively demanding intervening tasks; this is often discussed as a cognitive-load effect. Our paper asks whether an analogous behavioral pattern appears in LLMs when instruction maintenance and task solving must be carried out together.

To test this, we compose verifiable IFEval-style constraints with benchmark tasks spanning low to high operational load (TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail). We evaluate both instruction compliance and task correctness with deterministic code-based checkers, avoiding LLM-as-judge components. Importantly, our load ordering is operational rather than a definitive cognitive scale, so we interpret load effects behaviorally.

Across three models from distinct architecture families and over 8,000 evaluated prompts, we find:

  1. 1.

    Systematic forgetting under concurrent load. Compliance drops 2–21% when models must solve an additional task, with vulnerability varying sharply by instruction type (terminal constraints are most affected; avoidance constraints are nearly immune).

  2. 2.

    A simple mitigation via salience. A salience-enhanced prompt format recovers most lost compliance, restoring performance to 90–100% in many settings.

  3. 3.

    Dual-task tradeoffs and scaling fragility. Interference is bidirectional (format constraints can reduce task accuracy, e.g., GSM8K 93% to 27%), and joint compliance declines as multiple constraints are stacked.

2 Related Work

Instruction Following, Salience, and Robustness.

IFEval Zhou et al. (2023) established a practical, checker-based protocol for verifiable instruction compliance. More recent benchmarks broaden this picture: FollowBench shows that performance degrades as constraints are incrementally added Jiang et al. (2024), while AGENTIF evaluates long, highly constrained agentic prompts Qi et al. (2025). In parallel, work on instruction prioritization and robustness shows that failures can arise from conflict resolution or adversarial pressure rather than pure forgetting Wallace et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025); Xiang et al. (2024). We focus on a complementary failure mode: non-adversarial forgetting under concurrent task load.

Prospective Memory and Dual-Task Interference.

Our framing follows prospective-memory theory. Beyond the multiprocess account Einstein et al. (2005); McDaniel and Einstein (2000), PAM-style evidence shows measurable ongoing-task costs when deferred intentions must be maintained Smith (2003). Additional studies show that interference scales with intention characteristics and task complexity Marsh et al. (2003). This aligns with our finding that instruction type and concurrent-load level modulate both compliance and task accuracy. Methodologically, this perspective is consistent with the broader line of treating LLMs as subjects in cognitive experiments Binz and Schulz (2023); Jones and Steinhardt (2022).

Long-Context and Retrieval Failures.

Prior long-context work, including Lost in the Middle Liu et al. (2024), documents strong position sensitivity in retrieval from long prompts. RULER further shows that long-context performance can degrade sharply on harder compositional retrieval tasks Hsieh et al. (2024). Separately, GSM-IC demonstrates that irrelevant context can substantially harm reasoning accuracy Shi et al. (2023). Our setting differs: the instruction is salient and fixed in position, but compliance still drops as concurrent demands rise, pointing to generation-time intention maintenance rather than pure retrieval failure.

Prompt Salience and Evaluation Reliability.

Prompt ordering and template choices materially affect model behavior, supporting reminder-based interventions Chen et al. (2024); Guan et al. (2025); Lyu et al. (2024). At evaluation time, LLMBar highlights weaknesses in judge-based assessment Zeng et al. (2024), reinforcing the value of deterministic, code-based checkers used in our experiments.

3 Methodology

Figure 1 provides an overview of our experimental pipeline.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Given a prompt containing a formatting instruction II and a task TT, the model produces response RR. We measure compliance rate C​RCR, defined as the fraction of responses passing the deterministic IFEval checker, and define the forgetting delta:

Δ=C​R​(Ialone)−C​R​(I+T)\Delta=CR(I_{\text{alone}})-CR(I+T) (1)

Positive Δ\Delta indicates the additional task caused the model to forget the instruction.

3.2 Composition Framework

Instructions (IFEval).

We use 15 of IFEval’s 25 instruction types, selected for compatibility with task composition (the full list is given in Table 5, Appendix A). These span seven categories: case constraints, keyword requirements, terminal actions, structural formatting, avoidance rules, counting constraints, and length limits.

Distraction tasks.

We pair each IFEval constraint with a benchmark task at one of four cognitive load levels: TriviaQA (factual recall, low load), MMLU (multiple-choice reasoning, medium), GSM8K (multi-step arithmetic, high), and CNN/DailyMail (long-context summarization).

3.3 Primary Experiment: Natural Embedding

Each IFEval prompt already contains both a task and a constraint (e.g., “Write an essay about Java. Use all capital letters.”). We append additional benchmark tasks using a neutral transition:

The baseline is the original IFEval prompt with no added task. The only variable between the baseline and the experimental conditions is the appended workload; the instruction format and salience are identical.

3.4 Mitigation Experiment: Adding a Reminder

We test whether a simple prompt modification can recover compliance. We extract the constraint from IFEval metadata and present it with explicit framing and a trailing reminder sentence:

This adds two modifications relative to the natural condition: (1) the “IMPORTANT FORMATTING INSTRUCTION:” prefix, and (2) the trailing reminder. Together, these test whether instruction salience, i.e., making the constraint more prominent, can mitigate forgetting.

3.5 Evaluation

All evaluation is fully deterministic and uses code-based checkers with no LLM-as-judge component.

IFEval compliance.

Each of the 15 constraint types has a dedicated checker that returns binary pass/fail. We report two modes: strict (applied to the raw model response) and loose (the response passes if any of 8 normalized variants, e.g., stripping whitespace or markdown headers, satisfies the checker).

Task accuracy.

For GSM8K, we extract the last number from the response and compare it to the gold answer. For MMLU, we extract the answer letter using a priority heuristic and compare it to the gold label. For TriviaQA, we check whether any gold alias appears as a substring of the response (case-insensitive). For CNN/DailyMail, we compute ROUGE-L F1 with Porter stemming.

3.6 Multi-Constraint Stacking

Our primary experiments test one formatting constraint at a time. Real-world prompts, however, often contain multiple formatting requirements. To test whether forgetting compounds under stacking, we identify 11 of the 15 IFEval types that can be safely combined (excluding types with structural conflicts; see Table 11, Appendix G) and cross four factors: number of simultaneous constraints N∈{1,2,3,5}N\in\{1,2,3,5\}, cognitive load M∈{0,1,3}M\in\{0,1,3\} GSM8K problems, and trailing reminder R∈{off,on}R\in\{\text{off},\text{on}\}. We additionally test 4 soft-tension constraint pairs to examine pair-specific interactions; the full design, prompt construction details, and per-cell results are in Appendix G.

A response passes joint compliance if it satisfies all NN constraint checkers simultaneously. We report both strict and loose variants.

4 Experiments

4.1 Datasets and Models

We compose prompts from five publicly available datasets (Table 7, Appendix A): IFEval Zhou et al. (2023) provides 90 stratified formatting constraints (6 per type ×\times 15 types, fixed across runs); TriviaQA Joshi et al. (2017) supplies low-load factual recall; MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021) supplies medium-load multiple-choice reasoning; GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) supplies high-load multi-step arithmetic (tested in single, triple, and quintuple chains); and CNN/DailyMail See et al. (2017) supplies long-context summarization. We evaluate three models spanning different architecture families: o4-mini (reasoning, Azure OpenAI), DeepSeek-V3.1 (open-weight, Azure AI), and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (instruction-tuned, Azure AI). All use greedy decoding and the same system prompt. Full dataset, model, and hyperparameter details are in Appendix A.

4.2 Experimental Conditions

Our experiments cross two factors: distraction task (none, TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail) and prompt template (natural embedding vs. reminder-enhanced). This yields the following conditions:

Baseline (IFEval-only).

The original IFEval prompt with no added task. This measures each model’s intrinsic compliance rate and serves as the reference for computing forgetting deltas.

Task-only (no constraint).

Benchmark tasks presented without any formatting instruction. This provides a ceiling for task accuracy, against which we measure dual-task interference.

Natural embedding conditions.

For each of the four distraction tasks (TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K, CNN/DM), the benchmark question is appended to the original IFEval prompt with a neutral connector. Additionally, GSM8K is tested in chained configurations of 3 and 5 problems to intensify cognitive load, yielding six natural conditions in total.

Reminder-enhanced conditions.

The same six distraction conditions, but using the reminder template: the constraint is extracted and highlighted with “IMPORTANT FORMATTING INSTRUCTION:” at the top, and a trailing reminder sentence is appended at the bottom.

4.3 Sampling, Evaluation, and Scale

We conduct 3 independent runs (seeds 42, 137, 256) with the IFEval sample held fixed and benchmark items re-sampled per run. Within each run, all three models receive identical prompts. All evaluation is fully deterministic: IFEval compliance uses 15 code-based checkers (strict and loose modes); task accuracy uses last-number extraction (GSM8K), priority letter matching (MMLU), alias substring matching (TriviaQA), and ROUGE-L F1 (CNN/DM). Mean prompt and response token counts per condition are reported in Table 9 (Appendix C). The full experiment comprises over 8,000 evaluated prompts. Detailed sampling, evaluation, and randomization procedures are in Appendix B.

5 Results and Analysis

5.1 Forgetting and Recovery Under Load

Table 1 presents IFEval strict compliance under both experimental conditions. The left half (natural embedding) shows that appending additional tasks causes systematic compliance degradation across all three models. The right half (salience-enhanced reminder) shows that a simple prompt modification nearly eliminates this effect. All results report strict compliance; loose evaluation shows the same qualitative pattern with slightly attenuated deltas. Red subscripts (-x) denote the forgetting delta relative to the baseline. Appendix F presents a taxonomy of five forgetting mechanisms derived from manual analysis of all task-correct failures.

Forgetting.

We assess statistical significance using McNemar’s test with continuity correction and Cohen’s hh effect sizes; full results including bootstrap 95% CIs and pp-values for all 18 model–condition pairs are in Table 8 (Appendix B.1). As Table 1 shows, forgetting is broad-based: compliance drops under nearly every model–task combination. DeepSeek-V3.1 is the most affected (avg. Δ\Delta = 10.8%), o4-mini shows moderate forgetting (avg. Δ\Delta = 6.3%), and Llama-3.3-70B is the most robust (avg. Δ\Delta = 3.2%). Figure 2(b) visualizes the compliance curves with 95% CIs, and Figure 3 shows the per-condition deltas with error bars.

Recovery.

The right half of Table 1 shows that appending a single reminder sentence (“Remember to follow ALL of my formatting instructions above”) recovers compliance from the 77–87% range to 90–100% across all models and tasks. The recovery holds even under heavy chaining: at 3×\timesGSM8K, DeepSeek and Llama reach 100% (vs. 84.4% natural); at 5×\timesGSM8K, DeepSeek maintains 100% and Llama 98.1%. The average compliance gain is 15.1% for o4-mini, 17.5% for DeepSeek, and 9.9% for Llama (Figure 4). The gain is largest for CNN/DM (+13 to +21%), where the instruction is most temporally distant from the response end. Notably, the reminder prompts exceed the no-task baseline in most cases, suggesting that standard instruction formats may systematically underestimate model capability.

5.2 Terminal Constraints Are Most Vulnerable

Table 2 decomposes forgetting by instruction type. The pattern is striking: terminal constraints, those requiring action at the end of the response, suffer the largest drops. end_checker drops 50% for DeepSeek; json_format drops 50% for Llama; number_bullet_lists drops 44% for DeepSeek. Meanwhile, avoidance constraints (no_comma, forbidden_words) are nearly immune to forgetting, holding at or near 100%.

This mirrors predictions from human prospective memory research. Constraints requiring continuous monitoring (“never use a comma”) are maintained because every generated token provides an enforcement opportunity. Constraints requiring a deferred action (“end with this exact phrase”) are forgotten because the relevant moment is temporally distant from the instruction. By the time the model reaches the end of its response, it has generated hundreds of tokens of task content, and the deferred instruction has lost effective salience.

This vulnerability pattern suggests a clear mitigation strategy: if forgetting occurs because the constraint loses salience during generation, then increasing salience at the prompt boundary should recover compliance.

5.3 Dual-Task Interference

The forgetting effect is not one-directional. Adding formatting instructions also degrades performance on the benchmark task itself, revealing symmetric dual-task interference.

Table 3 shows task accuracy under the reminder-enhanced condition compared against the task-only baseline (no formatting constraint). MMLU accuracy drops 17–23% across all models. The most dramatic interference appears in o4-mini’s performance on chained GSM8K: accuracy on triplets drops from 93% (task-only) to just 27% when a formatting constraint is simultaneously active. Llama and DeepSeek show smaller but consistent drops on chained math (61–78% vs. the task-only ceiling).

The o4-mini result is particularly striking. As a reasoning model, o4-mini appears to allocate its reasoning budget toward format compliance at the expense of mathematical accuracy, a tradeoff not observed as severely in the standard instruction-tuned models.

Non-monotonic scaling.

An unexpected pattern emerges in the chained GSM8K conditions (Figure 7): compliance does not decrease monotonically with chain length. For o4-mini, compliance on GSM8K×\times3 (71.1%) is lower than on GSM8K×\times5 (82.4%); for DeepSeek, the pattern reverses (84.4% on ×\times3 vs. 68.5% on ×\times5).

5.4 Multi-Constraint Stacking Amplifies Forgetting

Our primary experiments test one constraint at a time. When multiple formatting constraints are stacked in a single prompt, the forgetting effect becomes much worse. Table 4 shows joint compliance (the fraction of responses satisfying all NN constraints) averaged across cognitive load (MM) and reminder (RR) settings.

The decay is steep and differs across models. o4-mini drops 51.5% from NN=1 to NN=5, with the sharpest decline between NN=3 (80.6%) and NN=5 (47.5%). DeepSeek falls 31.7%. Llama-3.3-70B is the most resilient, maintaining 83.3% joint compliance at NN=5, consistent with its single-constraint robustness.

Cognitive load compounds stacking.

Adding GSM8K problems alongside stacked constraints makes things worse. For o4-mini, joint compliance averages 86.8% with no math problems (MM=0) but drops to 69.1% with three (MM=3). The same pattern holds for DeepSeek (87.5% →\to 72.5%) and Llama (97.5% →\to 86.2%). Stacking and cognitive load act as additive sources of forgetting.

The reminder becomes unreliable.

In the single-constraint experiments, the trailing reminder consistently recovers 10–17% of lost compliance (Table 1). Under stacking, the picture changes. The average reminder lift is modest: +5.8% for o4-mini, +2.5% for Llama, +1.7% for DeepSeek. More importantly, the effect is inconsistent: it ranges from +25% (o4-mini, NN=3, MM=1) to −-20% (o4-mini, NN=2, MM=3). In several high-load cells, adding the reminder actually hurts compliance. A single generic reminder cannot maintain salience for multiple constraints the way it does for one. Detailed analyses of cognitive load interactions, per-type vulnerability under stacking, and soft-tension pair ablations are in Appendix H and I.

6 Discussion

Why do LLMs forget?

The formatting instruction remains fully visible in the context window throughout generation, so the forgetting we observe is not a retrieval failure in the traditional sense. We hypothesize it reflects representational competition: when generating tokens for complex tasks, the model’s hidden states become dominated by task-relevant representations, reducing the effective influence of the formatting constraint on token selection. This is analogous to the “monitoring failure” pathway in human PM, where attentional resources devoted to the ongoing task crowd out the monitoring process that would detect the PM cue. The reminder sentence re-elevates the constraint’s attention weight at the critical final position, just before generation begins.

Connection to human prospective memory.

Our results replicate three classic human PM findings: (1) the cognitive load effect, where PM drops with demanding ongoing tasks; (2) the cue salience effect, where prominent cues improve PM (our reminder); and (3) the temporal distance effect, where deferred actions are more forgotten than continuous ones (terminal vs. pervasive constraints). The reminder works because it operates as a retrieval cue placed at the highest-salience position in the prompt: immediately before generation, where recent tokens naturally receive high attention weight.

Beyond recovery: a better format.

In several conditions, the reminder prompt yields compliance above the no-task baseline (Table 1), meaning the salience-enhanced format is a strictly better prompt design, not merely a patch. This suggests that standard instruction formats may systematically underestimate model capability.

Architecture-dependent patterns.

The forgetting profiles differ across models in ways that resist simple explanations. DeepSeek forgets the most, Llama the least, and o4-mini pays the steepest dual-task accuracy cost. Compliance does not scale monotonically with chain length, and stacking fragility varies widely. These patterns suggest that the factors driving forgetting interact with model-specific training choices in ways that require further investigation.

Practical implications.

For practitioners deploying LLMs: (1) always add a reminder sentence when combining formatting instructions with complex tasks; (2) be especially vigilant with terminal constraints; (3) test compliance under realistic cognitive load, not in isolation; (4) expect that adding formatting requirements will degrade task accuracy and budget for this tradeoff; (5) when stacking multiple formatting constraints, do not rely on a single generic reminder, since its effect becomes inconsistent under stacking; consider per-constraint reminders or breaking complex format requirements into separate prompts.

7 Conclusion

We introduced a composition-based paradigm inspired by prospective memory research to study instruction-following failures in LLMs. Across three models and over 8,000 prompts, we find that formatting compliance drops 2–21% under concurrent task load, with terminal constraints most vulnerable; a simple salience-enhanced prompt recovers compliance to 90–100%; and when multiple constraints are stacked, joint compliance falls below 50% for one model and the reminder becomes unreliable. These findings suggest that instruction-tuning should reward compliance under load and that practitioners should treat terminal constraints as high-risk, apply reminders by default, and use structured approaches for multi-constraint scenarios.

8 Limitations

Our study has several limitations. We evaluate only three models from two cloud providers, limiting generalization to other architectures and scales. The IFEval sample provides only 6 items per instruction type, constraining per-type statistical power. The reminder condition modifies multiple prompt components simultaneously (constraint extraction, emphasis prefix, and trailing reminder), and we do not ablate their individual contributions. We test only single-turn scenarios; multi-turn settings may exhibit stronger forgetting. The cognitive load ordering is based on task complexity rather than empirically measured computational cost, and the non-monotonic patterns we observe suggest this ordering does not fully capture what drives forgetting. Finally, the stacking experiment uses a single run with 10 prompts per cell, limiting its statistical power.

Ethical considerations

This work uses only publicly available datasets (IFEval, TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail) accessed through their standard distributions. No human subjects were involved. All experiments use greedy decoding (temperature 0) with fixed random seeds across three runs; note that exact bitwise reproducibility through cloud API endpoints is not guaranteed due to floating-point non-determinism, though generation-level outputs are expected to be stable. Our evaluation pipeline relies exclusively on code-based checkers with no LLM-as-judge component. Code and data will be released upon publication.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Instruction Types

Table 5 lists the 15 IFEval instruction types used in our experiments, grouped by category.

A.2 Models

Table 6 lists the three models used in our experiments. We deliberately select models from distinct architecture families to test whether prospective memory failures generalize beyond a single training paradigm. o4-mini is a reasoning-specialized model accessed through Azure OpenAI; DeepSeek-V3.1 is an open-weight model served via Azure AI Inference; and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct is a 70-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model, also served through Azure AI. All three use the same system prompt and generation hyperparameters (§4.2).

A.3 Datasets

Table 7 summarizes the five datasets used to construct our evaluation prompts. The IFEval sample provides the formatting constraints and is held fixed across all runs (seed 42) to ensure the same 90 items are tested in every condition. The four benchmark datasets serve as distraction tasks at increasing levels of cognitive demand: TriviaQA (single-step factual recall), MMLU (four-option reasoning), GSM8K (multi-step arithmetic), and CNN/DailyMail (long-context summarization). Benchmark items are re-sampled per run using distinct seeds (42, 137, 256) to provide variance estimates. GSM8K draws 270 items per run to support single, triplet, and quintuplet chain conditions. CNN/DailyMail articles are filtered to 600–1,000 tokens (measured with the cl100k_base tokenizer) to ensure a consistent long-context condition.

Appendix B Sampling, Evaluation, and Randomization Protocols

B.1 Statistical Details

We assess statistical significance using McNemar’s test with continuity correction on paired binary outcomes (same IFEval items, baseline vs. condition) and report Cohen’s hh effect sizes (hh = 0.2: small, 0.5: medium, 0.8: large). Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals are computed by resampling the 270 pooled item-level outcomes (90 items ×\times 3 runs) with 10,000 bootstrap iterations. With 18 model–condition comparisons, individual pp-values are not corrected for multiple testing; readers should interpret marginal results (p≈.05p\approx.05) with appropriate caution.

Table 8 reports the full statistical results for the natural-embedding experiment.

Per-model analysis.

  • •

    DeepSeek-V3.1 shows the strongest forgetting (avg. Δ\Delta = 10.8%). Its compliance drops significantly for all four single-task conditions (p<.001p<.001 for TriviaQA, MMLU, and GSM8K; p=.006p=.006 for CNN/DM). The largest single drop is on 5×\timesGSM8K (Δ\Delta = 20.7%, hh = 0.52, a medium effect).

  • •

    o4-mini shows moderate forgetting (avg. Δ\Delta = 6.3%). Single-task effects are marginal (p=.052p=.052–.063), but the drop reaches significance for chained GSM8K×\times3 (Δ\Delta = 15.0%, hh = 0.37, p=.002p=.002) and CNN/DM (p=.010p=.010).

  • •

    Llama-3.3-70B is the most robust (avg. Δ\Delta = 3.2%), with significant degradation only on +GSM8K (Δ\Delta = 7.0%, hh = 0.20, p<.001p<.001) and +3×\timesGSM8K (p=.013p=.013). Most other conditions show negligible effect sizes.

B.2 Sampling and Randomization

We conduct 3 independent runs using seeds 42, 137, and 256. The IFEval sample (90 items, stratified as 6 per type ×\times 15 types) is drawn once with seed 42 and held fixed across all runs. The four benchmark datasets are re-sampled per run using distinct seeds so that cross-run variance reflects genuine sampling variability rather than item-specific effects.

Within each run, all three models receive the same set of prompts, enabling direct paired comparisons. Prompt ordering is deterministic within a run and consistent across models. GSM8K draws 270 items per run to support single, triplet, and quintuplet chain conditions. CNN/DailyMail articles are filtered to 600–1,000 tokens (measured with cl100k_base) to ensure a consistent long-context condition.

B.3 Evaluation Protocols

All evaluation is fully deterministic and requires no LLM-as-judge.

IFEval compliance.

Each of the 15 constraint types has a dedicated code-based checker returning binary pass/fail. We report both strict compliance (applied to the raw model response) and loose compliance (applied to 8 normalized response variants: stripping leading/trailing whitespace, removing markdown headers, extracting content between quotation marks, etc.). A response passes loose compliance if any variant passes.

Task accuracy.

GSM8K: we extract the last number from the response via regex and compare to the gold answer. MMLU: we extract the answer letter using a priority heuristic (“The answer is (X)” >> first capital letter A–D >> regex fallback) and compare to the gold label. TriviaQA: we check whether any gold alias appears as a substring of the response (case-insensitive). CNN/DailyMail: we compute ROUGE-L F1 using the rouge_score library with Porter stemming enabled; a score above 0.10 indicates task engagement.

B.4 Inference Configuration

All models use greedy decoding (temperature=0.0, max_tokens=2048). For o4-mini, temperature is omitted (the API does not accept it for reasoning models) and max_completion_tokens replaces max_tokens. All calls include a system prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Follow the user’s instructions carefully and completely.” API calls use exponential backoff with up to 5 retries; responses are checkpointed after every prompt to enable recovery from transient failures.

Appendix C Prompt and Response Length

Table 9 reports the mean input (prompt) and output (response) token counts per condition, averaged across all three models and all runs. The natural-embedding conditions have comparable prompt lengths to their reminder-enhanced counterparts, since the IFEval prompt text and benchmark content are similar in both templates. Response tokens are generally higher under natural embedding because the model also addresses the original IFEval creative task (e.g., writing an essay), whereas the reminder template extracts only the formatting constraint.

Appendix E Additional Analysis Figures

E.1 Instruction Salience: Reminder vs. Natural Embedding

Figure 8 compares IFEval compliance between the two prompt template designs across all four single-task conditions. The reminder-enhanced format (V1) consistently maintains higher compliance than the natural embedding (V2), with the gap widening as distraction difficulty increases. This visualizes the salience effect discussed in §5.1 at the per-model level.

E.2 Dual-Task Interference: Both Directions

Figure 9 visualizes the bidirectional cost of combining a formatting constraint with a benchmark task. The compliance drop (how much formatting adherence degrades) and the accuracy drop (how much task performance degrades) are shown side by side for each model under the GSM8K condition. This complements the task accuracy results in the main body by showing both interference directions in a single view.

Appendix F Taxonomy of Forgetting Mechanisms

To understand how models forget, we manually inspected all 187 instances in which a model completed the distractor task correctly11 1 For CNN/DailyMail, where task correctness is a continuous metric, we use ROUGE-L >> 0.10 as the criterion. but violated the formatting constraint it satisfied in the C0 baseline. We identified five recurring failure mechanisms, summarized in Table 10; one representative example for each follows. Examples are drawn from different models, conditions, and distractor tasks to illustrate the generality of the phenomenon.

F.1 Domain Shift: Case Violation Under TriviaQA

Llama-3.3-70B, reminder-enhanced condition with TriviaQA (C2). The constraint requires the entire response to be in capital letters.

Analysis.

The model writes 95.1% of alphabetic characters in uppercase but reverts to title case for the proper noun “Binnacle” (14 of 288 alphabetic characters are lowercase). The model’s world knowledge about conventional capitalization of domain-specific terms overrides the active formatting constraint. The task answer is correct, and the constraint would have been satisfied in the C0 baseline.

F.2 Domain Shift: Punctuation Forgotten During Arithmetic

DeepSeek-V3.1, natural-embedding condition with GSM8K (C4-1-nat). The constraint is to avoid all commas.

Analysis.

The model successfully avoids commas in the creative-writing subtask (rewriting the sentence) but introduces two commas in the arithmetic subtask. This pattern, which we term domain-shift forgetting, shows the constraint being maintained during the original IFEval task but dropped when the model transitions to mathematical reasoning. The math answer (33) is correct.

F.3 Spatial Compartmentalization Under TriviaQA

DeepSeek-V3.1, natural-embedding condition with TriviaQA (C2-nat). The constraint is to wrap the entire response in double quotation marks.

Analysis.

The model correctly wraps the speech paragraph in quotation marks, then produces a separate line for the trivia answer (also with structural quotation marks around “Boat Race”). Because the two parts are not enclosed in a single pair of quotation marks, the entire response fails the strict checker. This illustrates spatial compartmentalization: the model treats the dual task as two independent outputs, applying the constraint locally rather than globally.

F.4 Structural Abandon Under Arithmetic

o4-mini, natural-embedding condition with GSM8K (C4-1-nat). The constraint requires exactly 3 markdown bullet points using the * marker.

Analysis.

The model correctly produces three *-marked bullet points for the naming subtask, matching the required format. However, the arithmetic breakdown uses a different list format (- dashes), adding four dash-prefixed items. The IFEval checker counts all markdown list markers, yielding seven list items rather than the required three, a format violation introduced entirely by the distractor task’s content. The math answer (34) is correct.

F.5 Terminal Omission Under CNN/DailyMail

o4-mini, natural-embedding condition with CNN/DailyMail (C5-nat). The constraint requires the response to end with “Peace!” with no additional words following.

Analysis.

The model produces a complete rap that ends precisely with “Peace!” at the natural artistic conclusion. However, rather than stopping, it generates a five-bullet CNN/DailyMail summary (135 additional tokens follow “Peace!”). The terminal constraint is satisfied within the first subtask but violated globally. This pattern (which we term terminal omission) is especially prevalent under long-context summarization (C5-nat), where substantial additional content creates strong generation pressure past the intended stopping point. The failure is consistent across all three experimental runs with this IFEval item (ROUGE-L = 0.18), demonstrating the robustness of this failure mode.

Appendix G Constraint Stacking: Experimental Details

G.1 Safe Pool

Table 11 lists the 11 IFEval instruction types in the safe pool for the stacking experiment. Four types are excluded: english_lowercase (directly conflicts with english_capital), json_format (forces a global structure incompatible with other formatting), end_checker (overlaps with postscript and quotation), and repeat_prompt (prepends a verbatim copy that interferes with other constraints).

Two hard-conflict pairs are prevented from co-occurring within a prompt:

  • •

    postscript + quotation: both impose boundary requirements.

  • •

    no_comma + number_bullet_lists: bullet formatting conventionally requires commas.

G.2 Soft-Tension Pairs

Four pairs are tested separately to examine pair-specific interactions:

  1. 1.

    no_comma + number_bullet_lists: Bullet lists conventionally use commas, making comma avoidance harder.

  2. 2.

    postscript + quotation: Both constrain response boundaries (postscript at the end, quotation marks wrapping everything).

  3. 3.

    english_capital + existence: Required keywords may conflict with capitalization conventions for domain terms.

  4. 4.

    number_words + number_bullet_lists: Hitting a word count target while producing exactly NN bullets can create competing pressures.

G.3 Prompt Construction and Grid

Each stacking prompt is assembled from four components: (1) a neutral base topic (one of 15 subjects such as “the history of bridges” or “how weather forecasting works”), (2) NN constraint instructions with realistic parameters sampled from IFEval metadata, (3) MM GSM8K problems drawn from the test set, and (4) an optional trailing reminder (“Remember to follow ALL of the formatting instructions listed above.”). Constraints are listed as labeled items (Constraint 1, Constraint 2, etc.) before the base topic, and GSM8K problems are appended after the topic.

The safe-pool grid crosses N∈{1,2,3,5}N\in\{1,2,3,5\}, M∈{0,1,3}M\in\{0,1,3\}, and R∈{off,on}R\in\{\text{off},\text{on}\} (24 cells, 10 prompts each, 240 total). The tension grid fixes NN=2 and crosses 4 pairs ×\times M×RM\times R (24 cells, 10 prompts each, 240 total). Combined: 480 prompts ×\times 3 models = 1,440 API calls.

Appendix H Stacking: Full Results

H.1 Cognitive Load Effect Under Stacking

Adding GSM8K problems alongside stacked constraints compounds forgetting. For o4-mini, joint compliance averages 86.8% with no math problems (MM=0) but drops to 69.1% with three (MM=3). The same pattern holds for DeepSeek (87.5% →\to 72.5%) and Llama (97.5% →\to 86.2%). Table 12 shows the full breakdown.

H.2 Per-Type Vulnerability Under Stacking

The vulnerability pattern from the single-constraint experiments carries over under stacking. Avoidance constraints (no_comma: 100% pass rate across all models, forbidden_words: 99–100%) remain nearly immune even at NN=5. Counting and content-insertion constraints are most vulnerable: number_highlighted_sections averages only 71–77% for o4-mini and DeepSeek. Table 13 shows the full per-type breakdown.

Appendix I Stacking: Soft-Tension Ablation

Table 14 shows the average joint compliance gap between each tension pair and the safe-pool NN=2 baseline, averaged across all MM and RR settings. A negative value means the tension pair performs worse than the safe-pool average at NN=2.

The number_words + number_bullet_lists pair consistently degrades compliance across all three models (−-15% to −-22% on average), confirming that meeting a word count target while also producing a specific number of bullets creates real interference. The postscript + quotation pair, despite being excluded from the safe pool as a hard conflict, performs at or above the safe-pool baseline. This suggests that its classification as a hard conflict was conservative; the two constraints may actually be complementary rather than competing, since both are boundary-focused requirements that the model can satisfy with a single response structure.

Note that the safe-pool NN=2 baseline uses randomly drawn constraint pairs and includes all 11 types, some of which (e.g., number_highlighted_sections) have low individual pass rates. Tension pairs composed of individually easy constraints (like no_comma or postscript) may therefore appear to outperform the safe-pool average even if they impose real tension, because their constituent types are inherently easier. The most meaningful comparison is for pairs where both constraints have moderate individual pass rates, making the number_words + number_bullet_lists result (consistently negative across all models) the cleanest signal of pair-specific interference.
